Serotonin syndrome: agitation, sweating, tremor, clonus, hyperthermia.
SSRIs: Fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram — Hyponatraemia, serotonin syndrome, discontinuation
Serotonin syndrome features clonus and hyperreflexia and follows serotonergic drugs.
Combining these drugs with serotonergic drugs can cause serotonin syndrome.
Increased bleeding risk with NSAIDs/anticoagulants; consider serotonin syndrome with interacting serotonergic drugs.
Cautions: hyponatraemia (especially older adults), bleeding risk with NSAIDs/anticoagulants, QT prolongation with some agents and serotonin syndrome with interacting serotonergic medicines.

qs.q: Which oxazolidinone antibiotic inhibits the formation of the translation initiation complex by binding to a unique site on the 23S rRNA and carries a risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with SSRIs?
qs.e: Linezolid inhibits initiation complex formation and has MAO inhibitor activity, predisposing patients to serotonin syndrome. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone that targets DNA gyrase rather than the 50S ribosomal subunit.

qs.q: Which medication acts as a specific serotonin antagonist utilized in the management of serotonin syndrome?
qs.e: Cyproheptadine serves as a serotonin antagonist and is given orally to treat serotonin syndrome alongside discontinuation of serotonergic drugs and benzodiazepine sedation. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not serotonin toxicity.

qs.q: Which of the following agents acts by increasing the sensitivity of serotonin receptors to precipitate serotonin syndrome?
qs.e: Lithium works by increasing the sensitivity of serotonin receptors. Linezolid acts by inhibiting serotonin metabolism.

qs.q: What is the initial oral dose of cyproheptadine when used as a serotonin antagonist in the management of serotonin syndrome?
qs.e: Cyproheptadine is given at 12 mg initially orally, followed by subsequent doses every two hours until a clinical response is achieved. Smaller initial doses like 4 mg are not the standard starting recommendation.

qs.q: Which drug combination is most likely to trigger serotonin syndrome?
qs.e: Tramadol inhibits serotonin reuptake. When combined with SSRIs or SNRIs, which also increase serotonin levels, it can lead to excessive serotonin in the synaptic cleft, causing serotonin syndrome characterized by hyperthermia, clonus, agitation, and autonomic instability.

ai.clinicalScope: Serotonin syndrome in adult patients presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
ai.title: Serotonin Syndrome
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Serotonin syndrome is a drug‑induced hyper‑serotonergic state causing neuromuscular hyperactivity, autonomic instability and altered mental status. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria; prompt drug withdrawal and supportive care are lifesaving.

sections.p: An acute, potentially fatal reaction to excess serotonergic activity at central and peripheral receptors, most often after a change in serotonergic medication.
b: Use Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria – requires a serotonergic drug plus one of: spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus + agitation, ocular clonus, tremor + hyperreflexia, or hypertonia + temperature >38 °C.
Symptoms develop within minutes to 24 h of drug change or overdose.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the number of systems involved and the presence of life‑threatening features.
b: Mild: tremor, mild hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, mild agitation.
Moderate: pronounced clonus, hyperthermia 38‑40 °C, hypertension, tachycardia, confusion.
Severe: hyperthermia >40 °C, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, coma.

sections.p: Any drug that increases synaptic serotonin can precipitate the syndrome; combination therapy is the most common trigger in low‑resource settings.
b: SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram) – most frequently used antidepressants.
MAO‑I (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) – especially when combined with SSRIs or TCAs.
Linezolid – weak MAO‑I, often given for resistant infections.
Tramadol, meperidine, fentanyl – opioid analgesics with serotonergic activity.
St. John’s wort, herbal remedies, and certain antimalarials (e.g., quinine) used locally.

sections.p: A triad of mental status change, autonomic dysregulation, and neuromuscular hyperactivity guides bedside recognition.
b: Mental: agitation, anxiety, confusion, hallucinations.
Autonomic: diaphoresis, fever, hypertension, tachycardia, flushing.
Neuromuscular: inducible or spontaneous clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, myoclonus, rigidity (often in lower limbs).

sections.p: Laboratory and bedside tests confirm organ impact and rule out mimics; they are not diagnostic for serotonin excess itself.

t.b: Detect leukocytosis or anemia that may suggest infection or hemolysis; normal result does not exclude syndrome.
Elevated >1000 U/L indicates rhabdomyolysis; if unavailable, monitor urine colour and output.
Identify hyperthermia‑related dehydration or renal failure; treat abnormalities promptly.
Exclude infectious fever that can mimic hyperthermia; treat if positive.
Detect co‑ingestion of illicit serotonergic agents; not essential for management.

sections.p: Recognise features that herald rapid deterioration and require ICU‑level care.
b: Hyperthermia >40 °C – risk of cerebral edema and multiorgan failure.
Seizures or status epilepticus.
Rapidly rising CK → rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.
Hypotension or arrhythmia after initial hypertension.
Altered consciousness progressing to coma.

sections.p: Immediate cessation of all serotonergic agents, supportive care, and targeted pharmacologic antagonism.
b: Stop offending drugs; inform pharmacy to avoid re‑exposure.
Support airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen and IV fluids.
Control hyperthermia with external cooling; avoid antipyretics alone.
Benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam) for agitation, tremor and seizure prophylaxis.
Avoid anticholinergics and dopamine antagonists that may worsen autonomic instability.

sections.p: After resolution, review medication history and educate patients and prescribers to prevent recurrence.
b: Observe for at least 24 h after symptom resolution before discharge.
Document the offending combination in the patient chart and pharmacy record.
Educate patient on avoiding over‑the‑counter herbal supplements with serotonergic activity.
When restarting antidepressants, use a wash‑out period (≥14 days after MAO‑I) and start low dose.
Consider alternative analgesics (e.g., NSAIDs, non‑serotonergic opioids) in future.

sections.p: Conditions that share hyperthermia, autonomic changes or neuromuscular signs.
b: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome – rigidity is “lead‑pipe”, no clonus, develops over days, linked to dopamine antagonists.
Malignant hyperthermia – triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine, occurs intra‑operatively, genetic susceptibility.
Anticholinergic toxicity – dry skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention; clonus absent.

sections.p: Laboratory or bedside findings that may be normal despite severe syndrome.
b: Normal temperature early in the course – do not rule out syndrome if other signs present.
CK may be normal initially; repeat after 6‑12 h if suspicion persists.
Absence of leukocytosis does not exclude infection‑triggered hyperthermia.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent hypertension with tachycardia despite cooling

faq.q: Can serotonin syndrome occur with a single drug?
faq.a: Rarely; most cases involve drug interactions or dose escalation of a serotonergic agent.

faq.q: Why is clonus more specific than tremor?
faq.a: Clonus reflects exaggerated spinal reflexes from excess serotonin, whereas tremor can be caused by many other conditions.

faq.q: Is cyproheptamine always available in low‑resource hospitals?
faq.a: Not always; if unavailable, focus on supportive care and benzodiazepines while arranging transfer if severe.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man on fluoxetine for depression receives linezolid for MRSA cellulitis and becomes agitated with a fever of 38.8 °C – what is your immediate next step? — Stop linezolid and fluoxetine, begin cooling and benzodiazepine, consider cyproheptadine.
Which clinical sign most strongly distinguishes serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome? — Presence of inducible or spontaneous clonus.

A patient on tramadol develops hyperreflexia and diaphoresis; serum CK is normal. How do you confirm the diagnosis? — Apply Hunter criteria; a positive clonus with a serotonergic drug confirms syndrome even with normal CK.
Why is a wash‑out period required when switching from an MAO‑I to an SSRI? — To allow irreversible MAO inhibition to wear off and prevent excess serotonin accumulation.

In a rural clinic without laboratory support, how would you monitor for rhabdomyolysis? — Observe urine colour for myoglobinuria, track urine output, and assess muscle pain; arrange transfer if renal failure suspected.
What are the three pillars of serotonin syndrome management? — Remove offending agents, provide supportive care (airway, cooling, fluids), and give a serotonin antagonist if available.

A patient on St. John’s wort and sertraline presents with agitation and hyperthermia; what counseling should you give on discharge? — Advise against combining herbal serotonergic supplements with prescription antidepressants and review all over‑the‑counter products.
How does linezolid’s weak MAO‑I activity influence antibiotic choice in a patient already on an SSRI? — Prefer non‑MAO‑I antibiotics (e.g., clindamycin) to avoid serotonin excess.
